paragraphs.source_en: Kangetsu said, "He boldly chants such an unreasonable thing offhandedly, and yet it does not sound unreasonable in the least." The master cut in doubtfully, "Is that so?" Kangetsu paid no attention to this at all. He went on, "Why does it not sound unreasonable? If one explains it psychologically, it becomes clear. To tell the truth, whether one is in love or not is a feeling that exists in the haiku poet himself; it has nothing whatever to do with the crow. Yet his feeling that the crow had fallen for the woman does not mean that the crow had any such feeling; in fact, it means that he himself had fallen for her. When Kyoshi himself saw a beautiful woman bathing, he was startled, and at that very instant he must certainly have been quite captivated. Seeing, with his own enamored eyes, that crow sitting motionless on the branch and looking down, he fell into the illusion, 'Ah, that fellow is as smitten as I am.' An illusion it certainly is, but that is precisely what makes it literary, and moreover where its positive quality lies. To extend the feeling one has experienced to the crow without asking permission, and to do so as if it were perfectly natural, is that not rather positive? Well? Does my explanation satisfy you? Sir!"
